title: NEB Class 11 Physics — Elasticity — 2024
subject: physics
source: NEB Grade 11 Model Questions / NEB Past Papers 2020-2024

questions.question: Define stress, strain, and Young's modulus. What are their SI units?
questions.solution:
**Stress** = deforming force per unit area (F/A). SI unit: **pascal (Pa)**.

**Strain** = fractional change in dimension (ΔL/L). SI unit: **none (dimensionless)**.

**Young's modulus** = stress/strain within the elastic limit. SI unit: **pascal (Pa)**.
questions.knowledgeNote: Three moduli: Young's (tensile), shear/rigidity (shape), bulk (volume). Steel's Y ≈ 2 × 10¹¹ Pa.
questions.answer: **Stress:** force per unit area, F/A — SI unit **pascal (N/m²)**; measures the intensity of the internal restoring force. **Strain:** fractional deformation, ΔL/L — **dimensionless** (no unit). **Young's modulus:** stress/strain within the elastic limit, Y = FL/(AΔL) — SI unit **pascal**; a material's stiffness constant (steel 2 × 10¹¹ Pa, rubber ~10⁷ Pa). **Deep point:** stress has a unit, strain has none, and their ratio inherits the unit — that asymmetry is why Y is in Pa while strain is a bare number.

questions.question: A steel wire of cross-sectional area 2 mm² is stretched by a 100 N force. Calculate the stress. If Young's modulus of steel is 2 × 10¹¹ Pa, what is the strain?
questions.knowledgeNote: Convert mm² to m² (×10⁻⁶) before dividing — the commonest unit slip in this unit.
questions.answer: **Stress:** A = 2 mm² = 2 × 10⁻⁶ m² ⟹ stress = 100/(2 × 10⁻⁶) = **5 × 10⁷ Pa (50 MPa)**. **Strain:** strain = stress/Y = (5 × 10⁷)/(2 × 10¹¹) = **2.5 × 10⁻⁴**. **Deep point:** strain came from dividing by Y — the modulus's role is to convert the applied stress into the geometric response.

questions.question: State Hooke's law. A 2 m wire extends by 2 mm under a 50 N load. Calculate the force constant of the wire.
questions.solution:
**Hooke's law:** within the elastic limit, stress is directly proportional to strain (extension ∝ load for a wire).

Force constant k = F/x = 50/(2 × 10⁻³) = **25,000 N/m**.
questions.knowledgeNote: k = YA/L for a wire — thicker and shorter wires are stiffer.
questions.answer: **Hooke's law:** within the elastic limit, the extension of a body is proportional to the applied force: **F = kx** (k = force constant/spring constant, N/m). **Force constant:** k = F/x = 50/(2 × 10⁻³) = **2.5 × 10⁴ N/m**. **Deep point:** the force constant is stiffness per unit extension — 25 000 N needed per metre of stretch, and its large value is what 'wire' (vs spring) implies.

questions.question: How much energy is stored in the wire of the previous question when stretched by the 50 N load?
questions.solution:
Elastic potential energy U = ½Fx = ½kx².

U = ½ × 50 × (2 × 10⁻³) = **0.05 J**.

(Equivalently ½ × 25,000 × (2 × 10⁻³)² = 0.05 J.)
questions.knowledgeNote: This is the area under the force–extension graph — the same ½Fx triangle as the spring.
questions.answer: **Energy stored in a stretched wire: U = ½kx² = ½Fx** (for a linearly elastic stretch). **Substitute:** U = ½ × 50 × 2 × 10⁻³ = **0.05 J** (check via ½kx²: ½ × 2.5 × 10⁴ × (2 × 10⁻³)² = ½ × 2.5 × 10⁴ × 4 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.05 J ✓). **Deep point:** the ½ is the area of the F–x triangle — the force ramps from 0 to F during stretching, so the work is half of F × x, not F × x.

questions.question: Define bulk modulus and Poisson's ratio. Why is Poisson's ratio dimensionless?
questions.solution:
**Bulk modulus** B = −V(ΔP/ΔV): resistance to uniform compression.

**Poisson's ratio** σ = lateral strain / longitudinal strain: how much a stretched body thins sideways.

Both strains are ratios of lengths, so their quotient has **no units** — it is a pure number (between 0 and 0.5 for most materials).
questions.knowledgeNote: Rubber ≈ 0.5 (volume conserved), cork ≈ 0 — cork is why wine stoppers slide in without bulging.
questions.answer: **Bulk modulus:** the ratio of normal (volume) stress to volume strain — resistance to uniform compression: **K = −ΔP/(ΔV/V)** (pressure increase per fractional volume decrease); SI unit Pa; solids and liquids have large K (liquids nearly incompressible). **Poisson's ratio:** within the elastic limit, the ratio of **lateral contraction strain to longitudinal extension strain**: σ = −(Δd/d)/(ΔL/L); typical metals 0.25–0.35. **Why dimensionless:** it is the ratio of **two strains**, and strain itself is a ratio of two lengths — the units cancel twice over, leaving a pure number. **Deep point:** σ is the sideways price of stretching — pull a rubber band and it thins; Poisson's ratio is the exchange rate between the two deformations.

questions.question: A steel cable of cross-sectional area 5 mm² has a breaking stress of 8 × 10⁸ Pa. What maximum mass can it lift? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.solution:
Maximum force = breaking stress × area = (8 × 10⁸) × (5 × 10⁻⁶) = 4000 N.

m = F/g = 4000/10 = **400 kg**.
questions.knowledgeNote: Real cables use a safety factor (working stress ≈ breaking stress / 5–10) — NEB sometimes asks for it as a follow-up.
questions.answer: **Breaking stress** = maximum stress before failure = 8 × 10⁸ Pa. **Maximum force:** F_max = stress × A = 8 × 10⁸ × 5 × 10⁻⁶ m² (5 mm² = 5 × 10⁻⁶ m²) = **4000 N**. **Maximum mass:** the cable must support the weight mg: m = F/g = 4000/10 = **400 kg**. **Deep point:** the conversion mm² → m² (× 10⁻⁶) and the stress-to-force multiplication are the two steps — the cable's strength is a stress, but what it lifts is a force, and area is the bridge.
